claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure comprising dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Internal phase boundaries in the starting alloy produce dislocation pile-ups during room-temperature tensile loading.
Dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries generate local stress concentrations.
The local stresses associated with dislocation pile-ups promote microcrack initiation and catastrophic damage during straining.
Low-temperature post-solidification annealing can promote controlled segregation of a minor alloying species to lamellar boundaries.
Trace or deliberately added Nb or V will preferentially migrate to the lamellar boundaries during annealing.
The annealing treatment will produce a thin, solute-enriched layer at interlamellar interfaces.
The enriched interfacial layer will relax local stress concentrations.
The enriched interfacial layer will facilitate dislocation transfer or interfacial sliding.
Solute segregation will reduce the phase boundary's resistance to dislocation transmission.
Improved dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation pile-ups and their associated local stress peaks.
Reducing pile-ups and local stress peaks will mitigate premature microcracking.
The annealed alloy will exhibit greater room-temperature tensile elongation than the untreated alloy.
The annealed alloy will maintain or slightly increase its yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed response applies under room-temperature, quasi-static uniaxial tensile loading.
Lamellar coarsening during annealing may limit or negate the treatment's effectiveness.
An alloy chemistry that does not support effective interfacial segregation may limit or negate the treatment's effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis presents post-solidification annealing as the single intervention, but the intervention field also permits deliberate addition of Nb or V, which would constitute a separate compositional intervention unless the solute was already present.
